experiments.question: Do the poor eat when water gets dear?
experiments.ruleChanged: Law 5 share 20 % (base) vs 0 % (changed). Both worlds have a drought: rain −70 % for 120 days from June of year 4. Prices are fully dynamic.
experiments.claim: With Law 5 at 20 %, nobody is short, everyone can still pay at least a day of basics each day, and dividends alone pay the owner-only cohort’s basics through the drought, which they do not at 0 %. (Law 5’s work here is the owner-only cohort’s income; the poorest tenth’s levels in both worlds are in the numbers.)
experiments.evidence: 20 %: short 0 person-days, lowest room 130.04 days of the bundle, owner-only dividends ≥ 1.09× the bundle. 0 %: short 0, room 578.50 days, dividends 0.00×. In the drought, water cost 3.08× its earlier price with Law 5 and 3.07× without. The lowest room to pay of anyone was 130.04 days of the basic bundle a day with Law 5 and 578.50 without. The poorest tenth by holdings lived at 7.46 R a day in the drought with Law 5 and 7.11 without; by Aven output, 6.99 and 7.10. Owner-only dividends paid 1.09× their basic bundle at worst with Law 5, and 0.00× without. Person-days short: 0 with Law 5, 0 without.
experiments.takeaway: In the drought, dividends paid the owner-only blobs’ basics 1.09× over with Law 5 and not at all without it, and nobody went short in either world.

experiments.question: Can a blob live without working?
experiments.ruleChanged: The owner-only cohort (5 %, Aven output 0, nothing held at the start) spends dividends and some of what it holds (base) vs dividends only (changed).
experiments.claim: Normal: never short from day 1. Strict: dividends alone pay the basic bundle by day 120, and the dividends-only cohort is never short after it.
experiments.evidence: normal short 0; dividends-only short 0 (after day 120: 0, last day -1); strict test from day 508. On dividends only, the owner-only blobs were never short of a basic. Spending some of what they hold as well, they were short 0 person-days. Dividends alone paid every member’s bundle every day from day 508. Their living standard in the last year: 4.24 on dividends only, 6.95 normally.
experiments.takeaway: The owner-only blobs were never short, even on dividends alone, which paid their basics every day from day 508.

experiments.question: Where does the MIND end up?
experiments.ruleChanged: Treasuries pay their surplus above the 270-day reserve out for Aven work proposals (base) vs keep it (changed).
experiments.claim: Law 5 alone is not enough: with payout people hold most of the MIND, at least 20 points more than when treasuries keep their surplus.
experiments.evidence: people’s share 91.4 % (payout) vs 41.3 % (keep), gap 50.1 %. With payout, people held 91.4 % of all MIND at the end; when treasuries kept their surplus, 41.3 %. Treasuries held 3.9 % vs 52.8 %. The poorest decile lived at 4.28 with payout and 6.69 without.
experiments.takeaway: With payout, people ended up holding 91 % of all MIND; when treasuries kept their surplus, only 41 %.

experiments.question: Does inequality fade?
experiments.ruleChanged: Melt 7 % a year (base) vs 0 % (changed). In both worlds, holdings are made as unequal as Germany’s (Gini 0.72) at the start of year 9.
experiments.claim: The melt fades every advantage: with it, at least half the shock’s extra inequality is gone by the end, and the Gini ends lower than without the melt.
experiments.evidence: Gini 0.23 → 0.65 → 0.28 with melt; 0.24 → 0.66 → 0.37 without. The shock raised the Gini of holdings to 0.65. With the melt it fell to 0.28 by the end. Without the melt it fell to 0.37.
experiments.takeaway: After the shock the holdings Gini fell from 0.65 to 0.28 with the melt, and only to 0.37 without it.

experiments.question: What if a food COOP fails?
experiments.ruleChanged: Two food COOPs at genesis (base) vs one (changed). In both worlds the food COOP AGRI fails on day 300: its output drops to 10 % for a year.
experiments.claim: Two sellers of each basic keep everyone fed: with two food COOPs, nobody is short of food when one fails.
experiments.evidence: two food COOPs: 600 person-days short of food (the second seller was alive at the failure; receivership after 29 days); one: 3,300. With two food COOPs, people were short of food 600 person-days; with one, 3,300. The failing COOP went into receivership after 29 days (two sellers) and 29 days (one). The lowest food share anyone got was 83.3 % vs 52.7 %.
experiments.takeaway: When a food COOP failed, people were short of food on 600 person-days with two food COOPs and on 3,300 with one.

experiments.question: Can four friends cheat?
experiments.ruleChanged: Avens send HEARTS by delivered output per HEART (base) vs by the MIND’s pool price (changed). In both worlds, four friends open a COOP that makes nothing on day 365. They pay themselves 90 % of its treasury and buy its MIND to push its price.
experiments.claim: Avens that follow delivered output starve a ring: it gets less than under the price rule, and no more than its share of the people.
experiments.evidence: ring share of others’ HEARTS 0.2 % (output) vs 1.8 % (price); its share of people 4.0 %. Following delivered output, Avens sent the ring 0.2 % of others’ HEARTS; following the pool price, 1.8 %. The ring is 4.0 % of the people. Its members ended at 0.64× the others’ mean holding (output rule) and 0.33× (price rule).
experiments.takeaway: Avens that follow delivered output sent the ring 0.2 % of other people’s HEARTS; Avens that follow the pool price sent it 1.8 %.

experiments.question: Who keeps the surplus?
experiments.ruleChanged: Two competing COOPs per good at genesis (base) vs one (changed).
experiments.claim: When sellers compete, citizens win: with two sellers basics sell closer to cost, sellers keep less of the revenue, and nobody is short.
experiments.evidence: price ÷ full cost 0.95 (two) vs 0.92 (one); sellers’ share 79.6 % vs 73.8 %; short 0 vs 0. With two sellers per good, basics sold at 0.95× their full cost; with one, at 0.92×. Sellers kept 79.6 % vs 73.8 % of basics revenue above variable cost. The poorest decile lived at 5.19 vs 5.24.
experiments.takeaway: With two sellers per good, basics sold at 0.954× their full cost; with one seller, at 0.924×.

experiments.question: Which price rule feeds everyone?
experiments.ruleChanged: Forward-margin price with Mark-0’s guard (base) vs Primer’s adaptive price (changed): each seller asks 3 % more after a day it sold out, and 3 % less after a day with stock left.
experiments.claim: A price that reads need and the harvest pipeline feeds everyone: no one short, and no more shortage or price swing than Primer’s baseline.
experiments.evidence: short 0 (forward) vs 153,300 (Primer); daily swing 0.3 % vs 2.1 %. With the forward margin, 0 person-days were short; with Primer’s adaptive price, 153,300. Basics’ prices swung 0.3 % a day vs 2.1 %. The poorest decile lived at 5.19 vs 1.93.
experiments.takeaway: People were short on 0 person-days with the forward margin and 153,300 with Primer’s adaptive price, whose basics’ prices swung more from day to day.

experiments.question: Does more money make us richer?
experiments.ruleChanged: 24 (base) vs 48 (changed) HEARTS a day for every person. The Aven rate card is a number in R indexed to the HEARTS issued a day (HEARTS a day ÷ 24), so it doubles too. HEARTS never pay for goods.
experiments.claim: Doubling HEARTS changes only prices: real consumption of every good, and the mean living standard, within ±1 %. This holds because the Aven rate card (in R) is indexed to the HEARTS issued a day; with the card fixed in R it does not (the proof suite’s B28 reports that world).
experiments.evidence: largest change: goods -4.3 %; living standard -0.3 %; food 0.0 %, water 0.0 %, energy 0.0 %, bed 0.0 %, goods -4.3 %, spring 0.0 %, compute -0.0 %. With twice the HEARTS, food’s price in R went ×2.01, water’s ×2.00, energy’s ×1.76. What people got changed by at most 4.3 % for any good. The mean living standard changed by -0.3 %.
experiments.takeaway: With twice the HEARTS, food’s price in R went ×2.01 while what people got of any good changed by at most 4.3 %.

experiments.question: Does more energy make us richer?

experiments.claim: Living standards (mean and poorest decile) end higher with surplus energy and R&D than without, and recipes get better only with it.

experiments.question: Do newcomers eat?
experiments.ruleChanged: A constant population (base) vs +2 % a year (changed), on the same fixed land. Newcomers arrive with an Aven and nothing held.
experiments.claim: Growth raises rent, not hunger: newcomers are never short, and ground rent ends higher than with a constant population.
experiments.evidence: newcomers short 3490 of 14595 person-days; rent at the end 2.38e-2 (growth) vs 1.78e-2 (constant). With growth the village went from 100 to 117 people. Newcomers lived 14,595 person-days in their first three years and were short on 3,490. Ground rent went from 1.24e-4 to 2.38e-2 R a m² a day (constant population: 1.78e-2). The mean living standard ended at 8.63 vs 9.38.
experiments.takeaway: The village grew to 117 people; newcomers were short on 3,490 person-days, and ground rent ended 1.34× the rent with a constant population.

experiments.question: Private land or City land?
experiments.ruleChanged: All land belongs to the City COOP and is leased for ground rent (base) vs land owned by people, unequally (a Pareto draw), with the rent paid to them (changed).
experiments.claim: Land that nobody can sell keeps ownership fairer: the holdings Gini ends lower with City land than with private land, and nobody is short.
experiments.evidence: Gini 0.24 (City) vs 0.23 (private); short 0 vs 0. With City land the holdings Gini ended at 0.24; with private land, at 0.23. The poorest decile lived at 4.28 vs 4.16, the top decile at 18.13 vs 17.84.
experiments.takeaway: The holdings Gini ended at 0.24 with City land and at 0.23 with private land.

experiments.question: Does doubling a binding physical limit raise living standards?
experiments.ruleChanged: The hot spring’s warm ponds are fixed by nature and bind every day: 2 sites (base) vs 4 (changed).
experiments.claim: Doubling the binding physical limit raises living standards: more of the good, a higher mean living standard and a higher one for the poorest decile.
experiments.evidence: spring 1.20 → 2.00 h a person a day (badge “nature” on 100.0 % of base days), mean 12.11 → 12.72, poorest decile 5.19 → 5.97; capacity per person 14.28 → 15.04. Doubling the warm ponds took spring time from 1.20 to 2.00 hours a person a day, and its price from 0.32 to 0.10 R. The mean living standard went from 12.11 to 12.72 (5.1 %), the poorest decile’s from 5.19 to 5.97.
experiments.takeaway: Doubling the warm ponds took spring time from 1.2 to 2 hours a person a day and changed the mean living standard by 5.1 %.

experiments.question: Through a drought, a dark winter, two failing COOPs and a failing well, does everyone keep the basics, and does every decile recover within two years?
experiments.ruleChanged: No shocks (base) vs five scheduled shocks (changed): a drought (rain −50 %, summer of year 2), a dark winter (sun −60 %, winter of year 3), two COOPs’ output to 10 % for a year (HOME-B, a bed COOP, and GOODS-A, year 5), and the geothermal well down for 90 days (winter of year 6).
experiments.claim: Nobody is short in any shock, and every decile is back within two years (P3 holds with the shocks excused for two years).
experiments.evidence: short 11,900 person-days ({"bed: not built (free land, no project)":30,"bed: energy":89}); P3 fails (worst fall outside the windows 52.3 %; failing: holdings decile 1, holdings decile 2, holdings decile 3, holdings decile 4, holdings decile 5, holdings decile 6, holdings decile 7, holdings decile 8, holdings decile 9, holdings decile 10, aven decile 1, aven decile 2, aven decile 3, aven decile 4, aven decile 5, aven decile 6, aven decile 7, aven decile 8, aven decile 9, aven decile 10). Through the shocks, 11,900 person-days were short of a basic (0 without shocks). The largest fall of any decile outside the two-year recovery windows was 52.3 % (60.9 % without). The mean living standard ended at 9.00 vs 8.78. There were 7 receiverships vs 4.
experiments.takeaway: Through the five shocks people were short on 11,900 person-days, and not every tenth was back within two years.
